steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptually, a transformer is an architecture that learns to read a sequence of symbols (words, characters, audio frames, etc.) and produce another sequence (a translation, a summary, the next-token prediction, and so on) by repeatedly asking one core question: “When processing the current token, which other tokens in the sequence are most relevant, and how should their information be combined?”

Here is the high-level story, step by step:

1. Tokenisation and embedding  
   • Each input symbol is mapped to a dense vector called an embedding.  
   • Because the model has no inherent notion of order, a position encoding (a learned vector or a deterministic sinusoid) is added so the model can tell “first word” from “fifth word.”

2. Self-attention: the heart of the transformer  
   • For every position i, the model computes three small vectors derived from its embedding:  
     – Query (Qᵢ): “What am I looking for?”  
     – Key (Kⱼ for each j): “What content do I have?”  
     – Value (Vⱼ for each j): “What content will I pass along if someone wants me?”  
   • Each query Qᵢ is dot-producted with every key Kⱼ, yielding attention scores that say how much token i should pay attention to token j.  
   • The scores are scaled, soft-maxed into probabilities (weights), and used to take a weighted sum of the value vectors Vⱼ. That sum is the information token i gathers from the rest of the sequence.  
   • This happens in parallel for all positions, so every token can consult every other token in one shot—no recurrence, no convolution sliding window.

3. Multi-head setup = multiple perspectives  
   • Instead of one Q/K/V space, we create h “heads,” each with its own learned linear projections.  
   • One head might learn “syntactic relations,” another “coreference,” a third “verb tense,” etc. The outputs of the heads are concatenated and linearly mixed.

4. Feed-forward network (FFN)  
   • After attention, each position’s vector passes through a position-wise two-layer perceptron (nonlinear transformation) to let the model reshape information locally.  
   • Think of attention for communication, FFN for computation.

5. Residual connections + layer normalisation  
   • Add & norm blocks wrap both the attention sublayer and the FFN sublayer:  
     x ← Norm(x + Sublayer(x))  
   • Residuals make gradients flow; normalisation stabilises training.

6. Stacking = depth  
   • An encoder (for tasks like translation) is typically 6-48 layers of the attention-plus-FFN block. Deeper layers see increasingly abstract relationships.  
   • A decoder (for autoregressive generation) is similar but adds masked self-attention (can’t peek at future tokens) and cross-attention that lets the output sequence attend to the encoder’s outputs.

7. Training objective  
   • Commonly, the model is trained to predict the next token (language modeling) or the masked-out tokens (BERT-style). Cross-entropy loss between predicted distribution and true token drives learning.  
   • Gradients back-propagate through every attention weight, so the model gradually learns which patterns matter.

8. Parallelism and efficiency  
   • Because attention treats the whole sequence as a matrix operation (Q·Kᵀ), all positions are processed simultaneously, making transformers highly parallelisable on GPUs/TPUs.

9. Emergent behaviour  
   • Through large-scale training, the model internalises grammar, facts, reasoning heuristics, etc. Attention maps often highlight linguistically meaningful relations—subject/verb links, coreference chains, and more—without explicit supervision.

10. Intuition in a nutshell  
    • Each layer: “Look around, copy what’s relevant, then transform.”  
    • Stack many layers: early ones gather local context, middle ones discover medium-range relations, deep ones capture global meaning and task-specific dynamics.

That conceptual loop—“attend globally, then compute locally, with residual memory at every layer”—is what lets transformers achieve state-of-the-art results across language, vision, audio, and reinforcement-learning domains.
